[The spine of the week]{.kicker}

## Four components, one package

A4 is not one document. It is four linked components, each answering a different question. Polish here means each one answers its question clearly.

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.concept-card}
[1 · Practice Case]{.card-title}
The applied story: a real decision and what changed because of the evidence.

*Answers:* **what changed?**
:::

::: {.concept-card}
[2 · Research Brief]{.card-title}
The reasoning and evidence behind the recommendation, stated honestly.

*Answers:* **how do you know?**
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.concept-card}
[3 · Object Card]{.card-title}
The single readable artifact a viewer meets at the fair.

*Answers:* **what does a viewer see?**
:::

::: {.concept-card}
[4 · Reproducibility Capsule]{.card-title}
The inputs, steps, and files so the method can be inspected.

*Answers:* **how can someone inspect the method?**
:::
::::

---

## How the components fit together

The four components are not parallel deliverables — they answer four questions a reviewer asks in sequence.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    PC[Practice Case<br/>what changed?] --> RB[Research Brief<br/>how do you know?]
    RB --> OC[Object Card<br/>what does a viewer see?]
    OC --> RC[Reproducibility Capsule<br/>how can someone inspect the method?]
    RC --> A4[A4: Workflow Package]
```

::: {.reflection-card}
If a stranger can walk this chain without you in the room, the package is done. Networking is secondary — the package comes first.
:::

---

[Final polish]{.kicker}

## The semester spine, one last time

Every component must still let a reader trace the same six-part spine your A4 has carried all along.

::: {.spine-rail}
[Decision]{.node} [Evidence]{.node} [Variation]{.node} [Output]{.node} [Threshold]{.node} [Action]{.node}
:::

::: {.concept-card}
[The reviewer's question]{.card-title}
Can I trace **decision → variants → workflow → output → threshold → limit** across the four components without asking you to explain it out loud?
:::

Polish is not decoration. It is making each link legible.

# Visual-polish lab {.big-break}

Bring your weakest figure and your Object Card draft.

## Visual-polish lab

Work on one figure at a time. The goal is clarity, not ornament.

::: {.activity-card}
[Do this now]{.card-title}
Take your weakest figure and run the four checks below, in order. Stop when the key message is obvious in three seconds.
:::

| Check | Question | Fix if no |
|---|---|---|
| Message | Is the key insight obvious in 3 seconds? | cut clutter, label the point |
| Readability | Legible at fair scale, from a few feet away? | larger type, fewer series |
| Honesty | Are uncertainty and limits visible? | add range, caveat, or note |
| Consistency | Same fonts, colours, units across components? | align to one style |

---

## Object Card refinement

The Object Card is the one artifact most viewers actually read. It must stand alone.

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.concept-card}
[What it must carry]{.card-title}
- the decision and who it is for
- one figure that carries the message
- the recommendation, in plain language
- a stated limit
:::

::: {.activity-card}
[The 30-second test]{.card-title}
Hand your draft card to a neighbour. Can they state your recommendation and one limit after 30 seconds, without you speaking?
:::
::::

---

[Content refinement]{.kicker}

## Sharpen the writing

The Research Brief and Practice Case carry the argument. Tighten them.

::: {.activity-card}
[8-minute writing pass]{.card-title}
1. **Opening** — does the first paragraph state the decision, finding, and action?
2. **Thread** — is the stakeholder's relevance clear all the way through?
3. **Evidence** — is confidence matched to the strength of the evidence?
4. **Citations** — are sources complete and the capsule index linked?
:::

::: {.warning-card}
State uncertainty plainly. Overclaiming weakens credibility faster than admitting a limit ever will.
:::

---

[Message clarity]{.kicker}

## The message-clarity clinic

Pair up. One reads as a busy reader; the other presents the core message.

::: {.activity-card}
[Role-play, 4 minutes]{.card-title}
The reader skims, then asks: **"So what should I actually do?"** The presenter must answer in one sentence.
:::

::: {.reflection-card}
[The one-thing test]{.card-title}
If a reader remembers only one thing, what should it be? Does every part of your package support that one message?
:::

---

[Q&A preparation]{.kicker}

## Prepare for the likely questions

Most fair questions fall into three families. Draft one honest answer for each.

:::: {.three-step}
::: {.step-box}
[Method]{.card-title}
"How do you know the sample / model is adequate?" → state your check and its limit.
:::
::: {.step-box}
[Implementation]{.card-title}
"What would this cost or take to apply?" → give a range, not a guess.
:::
::: {.step-box}
[Alternatives]{.card-title}
"Could something else explain this?" → name the alternative you ruled out, and how.
:::
::::

::: {.concept-card}
A question is a chance to show your reasoning, not an attack to defend against. Acknowledging a limit builds more credibility than deflecting.
:::

---

## A useful answer, in four moves

::: {.activity-card}
[The response shape]{.card-title}
1. **Acknowledge** — "Good question about ___."
2. **Answer** — "Here is what I found / checked."
3. **Connect** — "What this means for your decision is ___."
4. **Offer** — "I can follow up with the detail in the capsule."
:::

Keep it short. A clear, honest answer beats a long defensive one.

## Reconstruct your weakest component in four steps

**Object this week: your weakest A4 component, as a reviewer will meet it.**

::: {.recall-4step}
::: {.step}
**Did** What does this component currently claim and show?
:::
::: {.step}
**Assumed** What am I assuming the reader already knows?
:::
::: {.step}
**Risk** Why is this the weakest of the four — what is missing?
:::
::: {.step}
**Verify** What one fix would most improve it before submission?
:::
:::

::: {.grading-note}
Post your four-step under your component. Posting + an honest reconstruction is the graded unit. Presenting is welcomed and earns credit; it is never required and never scored as performance. Volunteers go first; random draw may fill the remaining examples.
:::

---

## Triage what you hear

You will get more notes than you can act on before submission. Sort first.

| Priority | Meaning | When to fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | a component fails to answer its question | this week |
| **Important** | credibility or clarity gap | before submission |
| **Polish** | would improve, not essential | if time allows |

::: {.warning-card}
Fix one critical item well rather than ten polish items poorly.
:::

---

## Final submission checklist

Run this before you submit the package.

::: {.activity-card}
[Quality assurance — check each]{.card-title}
:::

| Component | Done when |
|---|---|
| Practice Case | what changed is clear, and who it was for |
| Research Brief | the reasoning and evidence are honest and cited |
| Object Card | recommendation + one figure readable in 30 seconds |
| Reproducibility Capsule | inputs, steps, and files let a stranger re-run it |
| Across all four | findings consistent, spine traceable end to end |

## Object Fair, the day

A calm checklist, not a performance plan.

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.activity-card}
[Before you arrive]{.card-title}
- test any display or files early
- set up the Object Card where it reads at a glance
- have the capsule index ready to point to
:::

::: {.activity-card}
[During the fair]{.card-title}
- open with the decision and who it is for
- let the one figure do the work
- answer questions in the four-move shape
- a few real conversations beat many quick ones
:::
::::
